summary: Defines the administration protocol for federated file systems. It gives administrators a set of interfaces for managing fileservers that take part in a federation, including creating and editing the links that stitch separate servers into one namespace.

plainLanguage.summary: The head librarian's controls for the shared library network: how to add a new library, and how to point a shelf at a book kept somewhere else.

questions: what is a junction in a federated file system
subtitle: The remote procedure calls an administrator uses to link fileservers into one shared namespace.

tldr.problem: Fileservers run by different administrators, often from different vendors, have no common way to be managed together into one namespace. Proprietary tools do not work across vendors or enterprises.
tldr.mechanism: The FedFS administration protocol is an ONC RPC program (number 100418, version 1) with procedures to create, delete and look up junctions, to set replication information, and to manage the connection parameters for a namespace database (NSDB).
tldr.outcome: Administrators get one standard set of calls to build the namespace, and NFSv4 clients that cross a junction are referred to the target fileset. Fileservers that act as internal nodes MUST implement seven of the ten procedures.

today: RFC 7533 is a Proposed Standard published in March 2015, and the unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. It works together with RFC 7532, which defines the NSDB protocol.

sections.title: Why Federating Fileservers Is Hard
sections.content:
A federated file system (FedFS) lets clients reach files and walk a namespace across many independent fileservers, possibly in several enterprises. Building such a namespace has been hard for two reasons: the servers are often in different administrative domains, and there is no standard way for them to present a namespace together. Vendor tools exist, but they do not help when servers run different software with no common management protocol.

RFC 7533 defines the protocol administrators use to configure the fileservers and build the namespace. It sits beside RFC 7532, which describes the protocol that lets servers from different vendors cooperatively build a namespace, and the requirements in RFC 5716.
sections.plainLanguage: Lots of file servers are run by different people, and each has its own remote control. This RFC gives them one shared remote control so they can act like one big server.

sections.title: Filesets, Junctions and the NSDB
sections.content:
The RFC defines its vocabulary up front. A fileset is a set of files and the directory tree that holds them, and it is the basic unit of data management. A fileset name (FSN) is a platform-independent, globally unique name for a fileset. A fileset location (FSL) says where one implementation of that fileset currently lives. Replicas of the same fileset share an FSN but have different FSLs.

A junction is a server-side link from a leaf node in one fileset to the root of another fileset. The namespace database (NSDB) is a service that maps FSNs to FSLs. A fileserver that sees a junction asks the NSDB where the target fileset is, and NFSv4 clients are referred there.

Fileservers that are 'internal' nodes of the namespace hold junctions. 'Leaf' nodes only host the target filesets and are not required to implement any of these operations.
sections.plainLanguage: A junction is a signpost on a shelf saying 'the rest of this is over there'. The NSDB is the directory that tells you the address of 'over there'.

sections.title: Data Types on the Wire
sections.content:
The procedures are carried over ONC RPC RFC 5531, and the data structures are written in XDR RFC 4506. The RFC embeds the XDR so it can be extracted with a short shell script.

A few types matter most. A FedFsUuid is a version 4 UUID in network byte order. A FedFsNsdbName is a hostname and port pair; the hostname MUST be a fully qualified domain name and MUST NOT be a network address, because FSNs are meant to stay constant. A port of 0 means the standard LDAP port, 389, so (nsdb.example.com, 0) equals (nsdb.example.com, 389).

A path (FedFsPath) is either an implementation-dependent administrative path or a path in the NFSv4 server's single-server namespace. The path / is encoded as an array with zero components, and no component may be empty.

NSDB connection parameters carry a security type: FEDFS_SEC_NONE means no transport security may be used, and FEDFS_SEC_TLS means StartTLS MUST be used, with a root certificate supplied as the trust anchor for that NSDB only.
sections.plainLanguage: Everything is written in a strict form, like filling in a form with boxes for the server name, a port number and a path. A port of zero is shorthand for 'use the usual door'.

sections.title: Junction Procedures
sections.content:
The protocol is the ONC RPC program FEDFS_PROG, number 100418, version 1. Three procedures manage junctions.

  • FEDFS_CREATE_JUNCTION turns a server-relative path into a junction to an FSN. The path must exist and be local to the server. The association MUST be durable before success is returned. It does not create the target fileset.
  • FEDFS_DELETE_JUNCTION removes a junction. The restored directory's permissions SHOULD match what they were before.
  • FEDFS_LOOKUP_JUNCTION reports the FSN a path points to. A resolve argument chooses whether to skip resolution (FEDFS_RESOLVE_NONE), use only the server's cache (FEDFS_RESOLVE_CACHE) or contact the NSDB (FEDFS_RESOLVE_NSDB).

Creating a junction where one already exists fails with FEDFS_ERR_EXIST even if it is identical. A junction anywhere but the last path component gives FEDFS_ERR_NOTLOCAL. Ordinary NFSv4 has no way to tell whether an object is a junction, which is why the lookup procedure exists.
sections.plainLanguage: You can put up a signpost, take one down, or ask what a signpost points to. The server will not let you put a second signpost where one already stands.

sections.title: Replication and NSDB Parameter Procedures
sections.content:
Three replication procedures work like the junction ones but apply to a whole fileset rather than one junction: FEDFS_CREATE_REPLICATION, FEDFS_DELETE_REPLICATION and FEDFS_LOOKUP_REPLICATION. They set the FSN that the server uses to answer NFSv4 fs_locations or fs_locations_info requests when no junction is involved. If a junction is being accessed, its own FSN takes precedence. The same FSN SHOULD be associated with all replicas of a file system.

Three more procedures manage how the fileserver connects to an NSDB. FEDFS_SET_NSDB_PARAMS creates or replaces the connection record for an NSDB. FEDFS_GET_NSDB_PARAMS returns it. FEDFS_GET_LIMITED_NSDB_PARAMS returns only the security type, which can be a less privileged operation because full parameters may hold sensitive data such as certificates.

Fileservers that act as internal nodes MUST implement the null, junction and NSDB parameter procedures, and SHOULD implement the three replication procedures.
sections.plainLanguage: There are also controls for 'this whole shelf has copies elsewhere' and for storing the phone number and secret handshake used to call the directory. You can ask to see only the type of handshake without learning the secret.

sections.title: Status Codes
sections.content:
Every non-null reply starts with a FedFsStatus. FEDFS_OK is 0, and a failed operation reports a different status, generally only the first error found. The values run from 0 to 37. Many names and meanings are borrowed from NFSv4, but the numbers are different.

The codes fall into groups: path and permission problems such as FEDFS_ERR_ACCESS, FEDFS_ERR_NOTJUNCT and FEDFS_ERR_ROFS; NSDB problems such as FEDFS_ERR_NSDB_DOWN and FEDFS_ERR_NSDB_AUTH; LDAP errors, some of which can return the LDAP result code; and cache errors such as FEDFS_ERR_NO_CACHE. With FEDFS_ERR_DELAY, the client should wait and retry with a new RPC transaction ID.
sections.plainLanguage: When something goes wrong the server answers with a numbered reason, like 'you are not allowed' or 'that is not a signpost', so the administrator knows what to fix.

sections.title: Security Requirements
sections.content:
The security considerations of ONC RPC apply. Fileservers that support this protocol MUST support RPCSEC_GSS (RFC 2203). Clients and servers MUST support its integrity and authentication services, servers MUST support its privacy service, and clients SHOULD.

The RFC strongly recommends an Access Control Service to restrict who can use the protocol, to prevent namespace corruption and protect NSDB communication parameters. When TLS is chosen for an NSDB, RPCSEC_GSS with data integrity SHOULD be used and access limited to domain administrators, since the payload provisions a trust anchor.
sections.plainLanguage: Only trusted head librarians should be allowed to change the signposts, and the messages they send must be protected so nobody can tamper with them.

sections.title: RPC Program Number
sections.content: A range of ONC RPC program numbers was set aside for FedFS: 100418 to 100421. Program 100418 has been removed from the reserved FedFS range and assigned to version 1 of this protocol, with the short name fedfs_admin and the description 'FedFS Administration'. The registration refers to RFC 7533.
sections.plainLanguage: Every remote service needs its own phone extension. This one got extension 100418.

items.label: FEDFS_NULL
items.desc: The standard null RPC; no arguments, no result.

items.label: FEDFS_CREATE_JUNCTION
items.desc: Create a junction from a path to an FSN.

items.label: FEDFS_LOOKUP_JUNCTION
items.desc: Find the FSN a junction points to.

items.label: FEDFS_SET_NSDB_PARAMS
items.desc: Set connection parameters for an NSDB.

items.label: FEDFS_GET_NSDB_PARAMS
items.desc: Read the connection parameters for an NSDB.

items.label: FEDFS_GET_LIMITED_NSDB_PARAMS
items.desc: Read only the security type for an NSDB.

items.label: FEDFS_CREATE_REPLICATION
items.desc: Set replication information for a fileset.

viz.caption: THE THREE RESOLVE MODES OF A LOOKUP

items.title: FEDFS_RESOLVE_NONE
items.text: Never resolve the FSN; returns an empty fsl list so the FSN can be seen even if resolution would fail.

items.title: FEDFS_RESOLVE_CACHE
items.text: Resolve only from the server's FSL cache; never contact the NSDB.

items.title: FEDFS_RESOLVE_NSDB
items.text: Resolve by contacting the NSDB; cached data MUST NOT be used.
